findings.explanation: The flagged line at lib/rucio/core/did_meta_plugins/filter_engine.py:299 uses str.format to interpolate `key` and `value` directly into an Oracle SQL string passed to sqlalchemy text(): `expression = text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@.{} == \"{}\")')".format(key, value))`. The `key` and `value` are NOT bound parameters — they are raw string interpolation into the SQL text, so they are not protected by the usual placeholder mechanism. Tracing the source of these values: the FilterEngine's `_filters` are populated from `parse_did_filter_from_string_fe(filters)` (filter_engine.py:61), where `filters` comes from `args.filter` user input (bin/rucio:601). In parse_did_filter_from_string_fe (lib/rucio/common/utils.py:1154-1220), each `and_group` string is split into `key`, `operator`, `value` tokens and stored as raw strings without any sanitization, escaping, or whitelist validation of the key/value content. The sanity check in `_sanity_check_translated_filters` (filter_engine.py:108-145) only validates specific well-known keys (did_type, name, length, created_at) and wildcard operators; it performs no character/whitelist validation on arbitrary metadata keys or their values that flow to the json_exists clause. Thus user-supplied `key` and `value` strings (e.g., a filter string such as `"foo == \")'; DROP TABLE ...--"`) can be interpolated verbatim into the Oracle SQL text, allowing SQL/JSON-path injection. Because the dynamic parts are neither bound-parameterized nor whitelist-validated, this is a genuine injection sink rather than a false positive.

findings.suggested_fix: Avoid raw string interpolation into SQL text. Use bound parameters so the value is passed separately, and validate the key (JSON path) against a strict whitelist/identifier pattern before building the query. For example, parameterize the JSON-path expression so that `value` is supplied via the text() bind-args mechanism (e.g., `text("json_exists(meta, '$?(@.\"<validated_key>\" == :v)')").bindparams(sqlalchemy.bindparam('v', value))` after validating `key` with an identifier/whitelist regex and rejecting values containing quote/path-breaking characters), rather than using `.format(key, value)`.
findings.semgrep_message: SQLAlchemy text()/exec_driver_sql() with dynamic content may allow SQL injection if user input is interpolated. Verify that only bound parameters are used.

findings.explanation: In lib/rucio/api/did.py list_dids_extended, the changed loop normalizes filters per OR-group. The 'scope' branch is `or_group['account'] = InternalScope(or_group['scope'], vo=vo)`. This overwrites the 'account' filter key with an InternalScope object (and deletes/ignores the 'scope' key). The same buggy line is pre-existing in list_dids (line 77, unchanged), which shows the 'scope' branch is a copy-paste regression: the original code (base line 106) was `filters['scope'] = InternalScope(filters['scope'], vo=vo)`. A filter that specifies a scope (e.g. {'scope': X, 'account': Y}) now yields a broken/mis-attributed filter where the scope value is interpreted as the account and the account value is clobbered. This is an authorization-relevant filter that drives which DIDs are returned, and the incorrect mapping can cause a requester to query the wrong scope/account combination. It is a genuine incorrect-condition defect on a changed line, but no explicit security policy text was observed that defines this specific rule, so it is reported as a candidate.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the scope branch to assign to or_group['scope'] instead of or_group['account'] (i.e. or_group['scope'] = InternalScope(or_group['scope'], vo=vo)), so the scope filter is preserved and the account filter is not clobbered.

findings.explanation: did_column_meta.list_dids builds the query by passing user-controlled filter keys (option NAMES) to FilterEngine, whose _coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute maps any string that matches an attribute name on models.DataIdentifier to that column and uses it as the SQL column identifier (attribute), not a bound value. This PR refactors list_dids to a 'filters' array-of-dicts shape and routes all filter keys through this engine (fe = FilterEngine(filters, model_class=models.DataIdentifier); create_sqla_query), so a key name that matches a model attribute (or, in non-strict mode, a raw name) becomes a SQL identifier chosen from attacker input rather than validated against a strict column allowlist. Because identifiers cannot be parameterized with %s/? placeholders, any filter key not restricted to the known DID column set could be used to reference arbitrary columns/tables, enabling SQL injection via the column-identifier path.

findings.suggested_fix: Do not derive SQL column identifiers from filter-key strings. Replace the hasattr/getattr coercion in FilterEngine._coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute with a strict, fixed allowlist of permitted DID column names (a whitelist map from key string -> explicit column object) and reject all keys not in the list. Only values (and never identifiers) should be supplied as bound parameters; validate filter key names against the known set before passing to FilterEngine.

findings.explanation: The refactored json_meta.py list_dids now constructs its filter query via FilterEngine (json_meta.py line 154: `fe = FilterEngine(filters, model_class=models.DidMeta, strict_coerce=False)`; line 155 `fe.create_sqla_query(..., json_column=models.DidMeta.meta)`). With strict_coerce=False, filter KEYs (metadata field names) and filter VALUES that are not coercible to a real model attribute fall through to the JSON-column branch in filter_engine.py. For the Oracle dialect, that branch executes raw text assembled with str.format from both the key and value: filter_engine.py line 299 `expression = text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@.{} == \"{}\")')".format(key, value))`. Both `key` and `value` are attacker-controllable (they originate from user-supplied list_dids filters / API/CLI filter strings, passed unchanged). An attacker can break out of the JSONPath expression via an embedded double-quote to inject arbitrary Oracle SQL. This is a newly-exposed path because the PR replaces the previous list_dids implementation (which used `session.query(models.DidMeta)` with bound `models.DidMeta.meta[k]` filters) with the FilterEngine path; the Oracle raw-text case in filter_engine.py is the code this section now invokes. (No allowlist is applied to key or value on this branch.)
findings.suggested_fix: Do not build the Oracle json_exists predicate by string-interpolating the user-controlled key and value. Either bind them as parameters (e.g. text("json_exists(meta, :jp, :val)") with a safely-built JSONPath that escapes quotes, or use an allowlist of known metadata key names and a properly quoted JSONPath literal with escaped quotes: value.replace('"','\"')) or, better, use Oracle's native JSON query functions via bound parameters so neither key nor value is interpolated into the SQL text. Apply an allowlist/validation to the metadata key name as well, since it becomes part of the JSONPath expression.

[README.rst:1-29] (relevance 0.04)
Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

[README.rst:1-29] (relevance 0.14)
Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

If you run the command below, the files are not in the RSE XRD3, but only in XRD1 and 2.::

    rucio list-file-replicas test:mynewdataset
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+
    > | SCOPE   | NAME   | FILESIZE   | ADLER32   | RSE: REPLICA                                   |
    > |---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------|
    > | test    | file1  | 10.486 MB  | 141a641e  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/80/25/file1 |
    > | test    | file2  | 10.486 MB  | fdfa7eea  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/f3/14/file2 |
    > | test    | file3  | 10.486 MB  | c669167d  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/a9/23/file3 |
    > | test    | file4  | 10.486 MB  | 65786e49  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/2b/c2/file4 |
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+


So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3
    > 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9


Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

    rucio rule-info 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9|grep Locks
    > Locks OK/REPLICATING/STUCK: 0/4/0


Now we can run the daemons. First the rule evaluation daemon (judge-evaluator) will pick up our rule. Then the transfer submitter daemon (conveyor-submitter) will send the newly created transfers requests to the FTS server. After that, the transfer state check daemon (conveyor-poller) will retrieve from FTS the transfer state information. Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

    rucio-judge-evaluator --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-submitter --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-poller --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-finisher --run-once

Now, ensure that the `.git/config` is proper, i.e., mentioning your full name and email address, and create the `.githubtoken` file that contains a full access token from `Github Account Settings <https://github.com/settings/tokens>`_.

Next, startup the Rucio development environment with docker-compose. There are three different types: a standard one to just run the unittests and do basic development, which includes just Rucio without any transfer capabilities. One slightly larger one, which includes the File Transfer Service (FTS) and three XrootD storage servers to develop upload/download and transfers capabilities. And a third large one, which adds the full monitoring stack with Logstash, Elasticsearch, Kibana and Grafana.

*Note: if you are running with SELinux enabled, you might run into problems. Check troubleshooting with SELinux on the help pages of your container runtime environment.*

Using the standard environment
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Run the containers using docker-compose (again might need `sudo`)::

    docker-compose --file etc/docker/dev/docker-compose.yml up -d

And verify that it is running properly::

    docker ps

This should show you a few running containers: the Rucio server, the PostgreSQL database and the Graphite monitoring.

Finally, you can jump into the container with::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash

To verify that everything is in order, you can now either run the full unit tests or only set up the database. Running the full testing suite takes ~10 minutes::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh

Alternatively, you can bootstrap the test environment once with the `-i` option and then selectively or repeatedly run test case modules, test case groups, or even single test cases, for example::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh -i
    tools/pytest.sh test_replica.py

[README.rst:1-29] (relevance 0.08)
Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3
    > 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9


Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

    rucio rule-info 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9|grep Locks
    > Locks OK/REPLICATING/STUCK: 0/4/0


Now we can run the daemons. First the rule evaluation daemon (judge-evaluator) will pick up our rule. Then the transfer submitter daemon (conveyor-submitter) will send the newly created transfers requests to the FTS server. After that, the transfer state check daemon (conveyor-poller) will retrieve from FTS the transfer state information. Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

    rucio-judge-evaluator --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-submitter --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-poller --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-finisher --run-once

[etc/docker/dev/README.rst:178-225] (relevance 0.06)
This container can be found on Dockerhub as `rucio/rucio-dev`, and the corresponding `Dockerfile <https://github.com/rucio/containers/tree/master/dev>`_ is also available. It provides a Rucio environment which allows you to mount your local code in the containers `bin`, `lib`, and `tools` directory. The container is set up to run against a PostgreSQL database with fsync and most durability features for the WAL disabled to improve testing IO throughput. Tests and checks can be run against the development code without having to rebuild the container.


I need a Docker based on another branch (not rucio/master)
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

In such case, you can download the Rucio container files and e.g. choose to modify the dev container before build::

    # in a different directory
    git clone https://github.com/rucio/containers
    cd containers/dev


Change anything you need, e.g. in the Dockerfile the code branch cloned to your docker container::

    # from
    RUN git clone https://github.com/rucio/rucio.git /tmp/rucio
    # to e.g.:
    RUN git clone --single-branch --branch next https://github.com/rucio/rucio.git /tmp/rucio
    # build your docker
    docker build -t rucio/rucio-dev .


Compose as usual using docker-compose::

    cd /path/to/your/rucio/clone
    docker-compose --file etc/docker/dev/docker-compose.yml up -d



Start the daemons
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Daemons are not running in the docker environment, but all daemons support single-execution mode with the --run-once argument. Reset the system first with::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh -ir


Some files are created. Let's add them to a new dataset::

    rucio add-dataset test:mynewdataset
    rucio attach test:mynewdataset test:file1 test:file2 test:file3 test:file4


If you run the command below, the files are not in the RSE XRD3, but only in XRD1 and 2.::

    rucio list-file-replicas test:mynewdataset

    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+
    > | SCOPE   | NAME   | FILESIZE   | ADLER32   | RSE: REPLICA                                   |
    > |---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------|
    > | test    | file1  | 10.486 MB  | 141a641e  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/80/25/file1 |
    > | test    | file2  | 10.486 MB  | fdfa7eea  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/f3/14/file2 |
    > | test    | file3  | 10.486 MB  | c669167d  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/a9/23/file3 |
    > | test    | file4  | 10.486 MB  | 65786e49  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/2b/c2/file4 |
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+


So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3
    > 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9


Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

    rucio rule-info 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9|grep Locks
    > Locks OK/REPLICATING/STUCK: 0/4/0


Now we can run the daemons. First the rule evaluation daemon (judge-evaluator) will pick up our rule. Then the transfer submitter daemon (conveyor-submitter) will send the newly created transfers requests to the FTS server. After that, the transfer state check daemon (conveyor-poller) will retrieve from FTS the transfer state information. Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

    rucio-judge-evaluator --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-submitter --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-poller --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-finisher --run-once

[README.rst:1-29] (relevance 0.12)
Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

Development
-----------

The idea for containerised development is that you use your host machine to edit the files, and test the changes within the container environment. Any change to files in your clone will be reflected into the containers by using volume mounts.

To see your changes in action the recommended way is to jump twice into the container in parallel. One terminal to follow the output of the Rucio server with a shortcut to tail the logfiles (`logshow`), and one terminal to actually run interactive commands:

From your host, get a separate Terminal 1 (the Rucio "server log show")::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash
    logshow


Terminal 1 can now be left open, and then from your host go into a new Terminal 2 (the "interactive" terminal)::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash
    rucio whoami

Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

[README.rst:1-29] (relevance 0.18)
Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

If you run the command below, the files are not in the RSE XRD3, but only in XRD1 and 2.::

    rucio list-file-replicas test:mynewdataset
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+
    > | SCOPE   | NAME   | FILESIZE   | ADLER32   | RSE: REPLICA                                   |
    > |---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------|
    > | test    | file1  | 10.486 MB  | 141a641e  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/80/25/file1 |
    > | test    | file2  | 10.486 MB  | fdfa7eea  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/f3/14/file2 |
    > | test    | file3  | 10.486 MB  | c669167d  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/a9/23/file3 |
    > | test    | file4  | 10.486 MB  | 65786e49  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/2b/c2/file4 |
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+


So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3
    > 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9


Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

    rucio rule-info 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9|grep Locks
    > Locks OK/REPLICATING/STUCK: 0/4/0


Now we can run the daemons. First the rule evaluation daemon (judge-evaluator) will pick up our rule. Then the transfer submitter daemon (conveyor-submitter) will send the newly created transfers requests to the FTS server. After that, the transfer state check daemon (conveyor-poller) will retrieve from FTS the transfer state information. Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

    rucio-judge-evaluator --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-submitter --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-poller --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-finisher --run-once
